reference.source: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Anterior knee pain localised to the inferior pole of the patella, typical of jumping and change-of-direction sports
Load-related pain that characteristically warms up with activity and worsens afterwards
A degenerative tendinopathy from repetitive high-tensile, energy-storage loading, not a primary inflammation
The single-leg decline squat reproduces and helps monitor tendon pain
Tenderness is maximal at the proximal patellar tendon at the inferior patellar pole
Ultrasound and MRI can confirm tendinopathy, but changes may be present in asymptomatic tendons, so correlate with the clinical picture
Management is progressive loading (isometric then heavy slow or eccentric resistance) guided by physiotherapy with load management, avoiding complete rest
Corticosteroid injection into the tendon is generally avoided because of rupture risk; shockwave and other adjuncts may help resistant cases
reference.pathophysiology: Patellar tendinopathy results from repetitive energy-storage loading of the extensor mechanism, as in jumping and deceleration, most often affecting the deep posterior fibres at the inferior pole of the patella. Cumulative overload exceeds the tendon's adaptive repair capacity, producing degenerative change with disorganised collagen, increased ground substance, neovascularisation and neural ingrowth, and little classic inflammation, hence tendinosis. A continuum model describes progression from reactive tendinopathy through disrepair to degenerative tendinopathy depending on the balance of load and recovery.
additionalDifferentials: Osgood-Schlatter or Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease in adolescents
additionalInvestigations: Single-leg decline squat and other load tests to reproduce and grade pain
Ultrasound to assess tendon structure and neovascularity
MRI to characterise tendinopathy and exclude a partial tear or other pathology
Comparison with the asymptomatic side, recognising that imaging change can be incidental
Biomechanical and kinetic-chain assessment of the ankle, hip and landing mechanics
redFlags: Sudden pain with loss of active knee extension suggesting tendon rupture
Night pain, systemic upset or a mass suggesting other pathology
Locking or giving way suggesting intra-articular derangement
Failure to progress despite appropriate loading
reference.prognosis: Often responsive to a structured loading programme, but rehabilitation may take many months and symptoms can be persistent or recurrent, particularly if training load is not managed.
pitfalls: Prescribing complete rest instead of progressive tendon loading
Intratendinous corticosteroid injection with its attendant rupture risk
Over-interpreting imaging change that can occur in pain-free tendons
Ignoring the wider kinetic chain and training-load errors
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
management: Base treatment on progressive tendon loading, beginning with isometric quadriceps holds for pain relief and advancing to heavy slow-resistance or eccentric decline-squat exercise
Modify training load with relative rest from jumping and deceleration rather than complete inactivity
Correct contributing kinetic-chain factors, including ankle and hip strength and landing mechanics
Consider extracorporeal shockwave therapy for recalcitrant cases and avoid intratendinous corticosteroid injection, which risks tendon rupture
Set realistic expectations of prolonged rehabilitation and monitor pain with tools such as the single-leg decline squat
Reserve surgery for symptoms refractory to a sustained structured loading programme
